comments.author: stefs
comments.text:
i'm also using a "type safe" templating engine (for kotlin, as a gradle plugin) of my own design that goes the other way - instead of embedding a model class into the template, a template class is generated that takes all the values as parameters.
i.e. MyTemplate.tpl.html
{if $foo}hello world, {$myname}!{else}goodbye, world.{/if}
which creates a kotlin class that can be used like this:
MyTemplate(
foo = true,
myname = "bar"
).toString()
the biggest upside for me is that this way there's full, free IDE support, i don't need to write extra view models if the mapping isn't 1:1 and performance is pretty good because in the end there's no runtime parsing/compiling/interpreting except for the baseline JDK stuff (though there are even faster engines).
https://codeberg.org/h34tnet/tempolin
warning: so far i'm the only user though, so don't use it in production. also, i'm working on some improvements right now which haven't been pushed yet.

comments.author: bob1029
comments.text:
> The request already reveals information about you; what browser you use, the language it’s in, the OS that runs it and your IP address, which the server needs to send you the response. That often reveals your location.
If we control the servers the clients are connecting to, I don't see how there could be much hope of hiding. We can spoof things like latency toward an upper bound, but we can never ever defeat the lower bound. Physics is still quite insistent about that one.
If we control
multiple
servers, we know where they are, and we can periodically compel our clients to rotate between them (see: DNS), we can engage in latency-based multilateration to put them on a real-world map. Depending on the number of servers and samples over time, this can be remarkably accurate. Determining someone's actual postal code just from network timing information is feasible.
VPNs obviously confound this in first order terms, but if we aren't careful they can make it even easier to identify our activity in other ways. We are trading concealment in the woods for concealment in a crowd. Both have their advantages and disadvantages. The VPN might also have a side channel that we aren't aware of.

comments.author: legitster
comments.text:
Every time this resurfaces I like to remind people that this is mostly impractical and not how things actually work at the commercial level.
Just because someone can theoretically demonstrate your fingerprint today doesn't mean you have the
same
fingerprint in a few days. It's that kind of stability that you actually need for consistent matching for advertising or tracking purposes.
90% of commercial fingerprinting services still rely mostly on the IP address. Once you remove the IP address, you're left with a set of configurations that have a very short half life - volume settings, installed fonts, software versions, etc. You can expect a good portion of your audience to degrade within a couple of days. (Whereas a cookie has a life of 2 years - practically though they only survive a few months).
What you actually pay for from third party vendors is a connection made around a more stable data point - a phone number, an email address, a user ID, etc. With one of these data points you can actually track people across multiple devices for as long as you want.

comments.author: adastra22
comments.text:
Very few people in the comments seem to understand what holography is. A hologram is not a “3D display” that mimics a sci-fi movie or TV show. A hologram is photographic media / display technology that records and transmits phase as well as intensity of incident photons. By capturing all the properties of the electromagnetic field that strikes the film, and re-emitting the same EM wave when stimulated, the hologram ends up being a full “3D picture” because after all, the light that hits your eyes ends up being the same as if you were looking at the actual scene. But that’s a consequence, not the defining property.
3blue1brown has a great explainer video on what holograms are:

stories.title_en: Local Indexing to reduce tool calling and token usage

comments.author: ryuuseijin
comments.text:
OK, so, I too have built a local index tool called slopdex [1].
It's very simple, parses the repo code and docs with treesitter, indexes it, vectorizes everything, then allows you do things like create a map of the codebase or do a semantic search.
One cool trick that does work well is the cross-search command, which allows you to do a duplicate code search using the vector index. This gets rid of a blind spot that lots of LLMs have that make it create lots of dupliclate helper functions. This works quite well in practice.
It has a few evals that I'm still working on, showing only modest improvements in token usage when using the map command, maybe around ~10% less. I think this can depend a lot on the type of task though.
Would be happy to hear any feedback.
[1]:
https://github.com/ninjaxtools/slopdex

Note that attestation can only be required during credential registration; at login time it's not possible to retroactively require attestation if it wasn't obtained during registration. And browsers will throw up a permission prompt if a website requests attestation. Are Netflix and Twitter currently requesting attestation when people register passkeys, and rejecting the registration if the user declines the permission prompt? I very much doubt it, since Apple's passkey implementation doesn't support attestation.
Therefore, the author's scenario that sites will wait until most of their users are using attested passkeys and then "flip the switch and start rejecting non-attested passkeys" isn't very plausible.

comments.author: bmitch3020
comments.text:
I've yet to voluntarily enable passkeys, for the main reason that I want portability, and not to be tied to any single device that can be lost. I want to be able to backup and lock my credentials in a safe. I also want to control the strength of my credentials for different services, and I don't consider my thumbprint used to unlock my phone to be as strong as a long password in a password manager.
The first time I was forced to use a passkey implemented within the vendor's app (3rd party password managers were not an option). I quickly closed that account.
The second time was an app that popped up a passkey opt-in in the middle of a bunch of transaction screens. I quickly realized the error, but there was no easy undo. The opt in was one green button in the middle of the screen. Turning it back off required digging through settings to find the security option to disable, and then confirm my choice multiple times. That process also signed out all my other devices.
The fact that companies are resorting to dark patterns and forced requirements, where my money is held hostage, should be pretty good evidence of how poorly the passkey rollout is going.

comments.author: Animats
comments.text:
Since 1996, the NEMA 10 column (10-20, 10-30) is no longer allowed in new installations.
That was, for decades, the standard dryer outlet. No ground. The frame of the dryer is grounded to the neutral! Not to protective ground.
This is idiotic by modern standards, but is still found in older houses.
(Haven't had to look at the NEMA outlet chart in years. I once had to specify a computer room back when DEC was a company. DEC used about five different connectors - some 110V, some 220V, some 3-phase, various current ratings.
Needed custom-fabricated raceways with all the correct outlets.
Plus the
electrical people at the aerospace company insisted on putting a hulking big copper busbar tied to ground on top of each raceway, and all cabinets were grounded to that.
That was to give RF noise a very low resistance path to ground. Much RF R&D took place in that building, and things which blithered all over the RF spectrum were seriously annoying to the RF engineers. Computer grounding used to be a big deal, before everybody started using differential signals for almost everything.)
